name: The Five Oceans
teaser: Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern, Arctic: the Pacific alone covers more area than all land combined. Earth is an ocean planet — 71% of its surface is water, and we've explored less than 5%.

exploreAction.targetName: The world's five oceans and their sizes
exploreAction.instruction: Compare the sizes of all five oceans, then explain why the Southern Ocean was only officially recognized in 2021.

name: The Pacific Ocean
teaser: The largest and deepest ocean: the Pacific covers 63 million square miles, contains more than half the world's open water, and holds the Mariana Trench — the deepest point on Earth.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the Mariana Trench (11,034m deep), the Ring of Fire, and the Great Pacific Garbage Patch, then explain why the Pacific is shrinking.

name: The Atlantic Ocean
teaser: The second-largest ocean, dividing the Old and New Worlds: the Atlantic is growing as the Mid-Atlantic Ridge pushes tectonic plates apart. Its currents regulate climate across three continents.

exploreAction.targetName: How the Atlantic shapes global climate
exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the Gulf Stream and Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC), then explain why AMOC slowdown could trigger European cooling.

name: The Mariana Trench
teaser: At 11,034 meters deep, the Challenger Deep is the deepest known point on Earth. Pressure at the bottom is 1,000 times surface atmospheric — yet life thrives in total darkness.

exploreAction.targetName: Life at the bottom of the ocean
exploreAction.instruction: Learn about hadal zone creatures (snailfish, amphipods, xenophyophores), then explain how organisms survive crushing pressure, freezing temperatures, and total darkness.

name: Mid-Ocean Ridges
teaser: A 65,000 km underwater mountain range where tectonic plates diverge: new ocean floor is born at mid-ocean ridges. It's the longest mountain chain on Earth — and almost nobody's seen it.

exploreAction.targetName: How new ocean floor is created
exploreAction.instruction: Learn about seafloor spreading and hydrothermal vents at mid-ocean ridges, then explain how this process drives plate tectonics.

name: Hydrothermal Vents
teaser: Black smokers spewing 400°C mineral-rich water: hydrothermal vents support entire ecosystems without sunlight. Bacteria here use chemosynthesis instead of photosynthesis — a completely different basis for life.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about chemosynthetic bacteria, giant tube worms, and vent crabs, then explain how vent ecosystems challenged the assumption that all life needs sunlight.

name: The Great Barrier Reef
teaser: The largest living structure on Earth: 2,300 km of coral stretching along Australia's coast, visible from space. It hosts 1,500 fish species and 400 coral types — but bleaching is killing it.

exploreAction.targetName: Why coral bleaching is killing the reef
exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the coral-zooxanthellae symbiosis, then explain how rising ocean temperatures trigger mass bleaching events.

name: Coral Reef Ecosystems
teaser: Coral reefs cover less than 1% of the ocean floor but support 25% of all marine species. They're called 'rainforests of the sea' — and they're disappearing three times faster than rainforests.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the economic value of coral reefs (fisheries, tourism, coastal protection), then find one reef system outside Australia that's critically endangered.

name: Kelp Forests
teaser: Underwater jungles of giant kelp can grow 60 cm per day, creating three-dimensional habitats for sea otters, fish, and invertebrates. Kelp absorbs carbon 20 times faster than land forests.

exploreAction.targetName: How kelp forests support marine life
exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the kelp-urchin-otter trophic cascade, then explain why kelp forests are considered a nature-based climate solution.

name: The Open Ocean (Pelagic Zone)
teaser: The vast blue emptiness — or so it seems: the pelagic zone is the largest habitat on Earth, and it's full of life adapted to life without walls. Phytoplankton here produce half the world's oxygen.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the different pelagic zones (epipelagic, mesopelagic, bathypelagic), then explain why the open ocean is the least productive habitat per square meter.

name: The Abyssal Zone
teaser: Below 4,000 meters: eternal darkness, near-freezing temperatures, and crushing pressure. Yet life persists — transparent fish, bioluminescent jellyfish, and xenophyophores the size of grapefruits.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about adaptations to the abyss (bioluminescence, antifreeze proteins, pressure-resistant membranes), then find one deep-sea creature that looks like science fiction.

name: Ocean Currents
teaser: The ocean's conveyor belt: surface currents driven by wind and deep currents driven by temperature and salinity. They transport heat from the equator to the poles — regulating Earth's climate.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how temperature and salinity drive the global ocean conveyor belt, then explain why melting Arctic ice could shut down the Gulf Stream.

name: El Niño and La Niña
teaser: Every 2-7 years, Pacific Ocean temperatures swing between warm (El Niño) and cool (La Niña), disrupting weather worldwide. Droughts in Australia, floods in Peru, weaker hurricanes in the Atlantic.

exploreAction.targetName: How El Niño affects global weather
exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO), then find three countries affected differently by the same El Niño event.

name: Tides
teaser: The ocean breathes: tides rise and fall as the Moon's gravity pulls on Earth's water. The Bay of Fundy sees a 16-meter tidal range — the water level changes by the height of a five-story building.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why there are two high tides per day and how spring/neap tides relate to the Sun and Moon, then explain why the Bay of Fundy has such extreme tides.

name: Ocean Waves
teaser: Wind, gravity, and distant storms create waves that travel thousands of miles. A wave that hits California may have been born in a Antarctic storm. Surfers ride energy, not water.

exploreAction.targetName: How ocean waves form and travel
exploreAction.instruction: Learn about wave generation (wind speed, duration, fetch), then explain why deep-water waves don't actually move water forward.

name: Tsunamis
teaser: Underwater earthquakes, landslides, or volcanic eruptions generate waves that cross entire ocean basins at jet speed. The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami killed 230,000 people in hours.

exploreAction.targetName: How tsunamis form and how warning systems work
exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the earthquake-tsunami mechanism and the DART buoy warning system, then explain why tsunamis are invisible in deep water.

name: Whale Migration
teaser: Gray whales travel 10,000 km each way between Alaska and Mexico. Humpbacks cross entire ocean basins. The longest animal migration on Earth happens underwater.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about gray whale and humpback whale migration routes, then explain why whales migrate and how they navigate.

name: The Giant Squid
teaser: For centuries, sailors told stories of sea monsters. The giant squid (Architeuthis) is real: 13 meters long, with the largest eyes in the animal kingdom. It wasn't photographed alive until 2004.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about giant squid anatomy (giant eyes for deep-sea vision, two-third-length tentacles), then explain why they were so hard to photograph alive.

name: The Blue Whale
teaser: The largest animal that has ever lived: 30 meters long, 150 tons, with a heart the size of a small car. Blue whales eat 4 tons of krill daily and communicate across hundreds of kilometers.

exploreAction.targetName: The scale of the blue whale
exploreAction.instruction: Compare blue whale dimensions to everyday objects (heart = small car, tongue = elephant), then explain how whaling almost drove them extinct and their current recovery status.

name: Bioluminescence
teaser: Living light: 76% of deep-sea creatures produce their own glow. Anglerfish lure prey with it, dinoflagellates create blue waves on beaches, and some squid use it for camouflage.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the functions of bioluminescence (predation, defense, communication), then find one bioluminescent event you could witness in person.

name: Oil Spills
teaser: Deepwater Horizon (2010) spilled 780 million liters of oil into the Gulf of Mexico. The cleanup took years; the ecological damage will last decades. Oil and water don't mix — and neither do oil and ecosystems.

exploreAction.targetName: The impact of oil spills on marine life
exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the Deepwater Horizon spill's effects on marine ecosystems, then explain why dispersants are controversial.

name: Ocean Plastic Pollution
teaser: 8 million tons of plastic enter the ocean every year. It's in the Mariana Trench, in Arctic ice, and in the stomachs of 90% of seabirds. Microplastics are now in the food chain — including yours.

exploreAction.targetName: Where ocean plastic comes from and where it goes
exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the Great Pacific Garbage Patch and microplastics, then find one action that reduces plastic entering the ocean.

name: Overfishing
teaser: 90% of large predatory fish are gone. Industrial fishing fleets with sonar and GPS have stripped the ocean faster than it can recover. Some fish stocks have collapsed by 99%.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about maximum sustainable yield and bycatch, then find one fish species that's currently overfished and one that's recovering.

name: Ocean Acidification
teaser: The ocean absorbs 30% of human CO₂ emissions — but this makes seawater more acidic.珊瑚 dissolves, shellfish struggle, and the entire marine food web is at risk. It's called 'climate change's equally evil twin.'

exploreAction.targetName: How CO₂ is changing ocean chemistry
exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the carbonate chemistry of acidification, then explain why coral reefs and shellfish are especially vulnerable.

name: Captain Cook's Voyages
teaser: Between 1768 and 1779, Cook circumnavigated the globe, mapped Australia, discovered Hawaii, and transformed European knowledge of the Pacific. He was also a pioneer of navigation science.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about Cook's use of the transit of Venus for navigation and his encounters with Pacific Island cultures, then evaluate his legacy.

name: The Trieste Dive to the Challenger Deep
teaser: In 1960, Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh descended to the bottom of the Mariana Trench in the bathyscaphe Trieste: 10,916 meters. They spent 20 minutes on the floor and saw a flatfish.

exploreAction.targetName: The first dive to the deepest point
exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the Trieste's design and the extreme engineering challenges, then compare with James Cameron's 2012 solo dive.

name: HMS Beagle and Darwin
teaser: The five-year voyage of the Beagle (1831–1836) carried young Charles Darwin around the world. His observations of finches, tortoises, and fossils in the Galápagos laid the groundwork for evolution.

exploreAction.targetName: What Darwin saw on the Beagle
exploreAction.instruction: Learn about Darwin's observations in the Galápagos, then explain how oceanography and biology intersected on a single voyage.

name: The USS Nautilus and Submarine Exploration
teaser: The first nuclear-powered submarine: Nautilus crossed the North Pole underwater in 1958, proving that submarines could operate for months without surfacing. It changed warfare and oceanography forever.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the Nautilus's nuclear propulsion and its Arctic crossing, then explain how submarines use sonar for navigation.

name: Seamounts
teaser: Underwater mountains: there are more than 100,000 seamounts taller than 1,000 meters. They create ocean currents, concentrate marine life, and may influence weather patterns.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the Taylor column effect (how seamounts trap water and nutrients), then find one seamount that's a marine protected area.

name: Ocean Depth Zones
teaser: Sunlight (0-200m), twilight (200-1000m), midnight (1000-4000m), abyssal (4000-6000m), hadal (6000m+): each zone has its own rules for light, pressure, and life.

exploreAction.targetName: Life in each ocean depth zone
exploreAction.instruction: Learn the characteristics of each zone (photic, dysphotic, aphotic), then find one creature adapted to each zone.

name: Sea Level Rise
teaser: The ocean is rising 3.6 mm per year and accelerating. By 2100, it could rise 1 meter — flooding coastal cities, displacing 200 million people, and redefining where humans can live.

exploreAction.targetName: How fast the ocean is rising
exploreAction.instruction: Learn about thermal expansion and ice sheet melting as drivers of sea level rise, then find three major cities at risk.

name: Coral Spawning
teaser: Once a year, after a full moon, coral colonies release millions of eggs and sperm simultaneously: an underwater blizzard of pink and orange. It's one of nature's most synchronized events.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the environmental cues (temperature, moonlight, tidal cycles) that trigger mass spawning, then find one location where you can witness it.

name: Whale Songs
teaser: Humpback whale songs last up to 20 minutes and travel thousands of kilometers. Each population shares a song that evolves over years. Scientists still don't know exactly why they sing.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about humpback song structure and how songs spread between populations, then debate the leading theories for why whales sing.

name: Deep-Sea Mining
teaser: The ocean floor holds polymetallic nodules rich in cobalt, manganese, and rare earths. Companies want to mine them — but scientists warn that we could destroy ecosystems we haven't even discovered yet.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about polymetallic nodules and the International Seabed Authority, then debate whether deep-sea mining is necessary for the green energy transition.

name: Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion
teaser: Using the temperature difference between warm surface water and cold deep water to generate electricity: OTEC works in the tropics and could provide baseload renewable power to island nations.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the Rankine cycle原理 behind OTEC, then explain why it only works in tropical waters and why it hasn't scaled yet.

name: Mangrove Forests
teaser: Trees that grow in saltwater: mangroves protect coastlines from storms, store 4x more carbon than rainforests, and nursery grounds for 75% of commercial fish species. They're the ocean's unsung heroes.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about mangrove root systems and their role in coastal protection, then find one country that's successfully restoring mangroves.

name: Seagrass Meadows
teaser: Underwater grasslands that feed dugongs, shelter juvenile fish, and sequester carbon 35 times faster than rainforests. Seagrass covers 0.1% of the ocean floor but supports 20% of marine biodiversity.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about blue carbon sequestration by seagrass, then explain why seagrass meadows are declining globally.

name: Ocean Trenches
teaser: Subduction zones where one tectonic plate dives beneath another: ocean trenches are the deepest parts of the ocean. The Pacific Ring of Fire contains most of them — and some are volcanically active.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the ten deepest trenches and their locations, then explain why trenches form at subduction zones.

name: Global Shipping Lanes
teaser: 90% of world trade moves by sea: container ships, tankers, and bulk carriers follow invisible highways across the ocean. A single ship can carry 20,000 containers — enough to fill a small town.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about containerization and global shipping routes, then explain why the Suez Canal blockage in 2021 disrupted global supply chains.

name: Shipwrecks
teaser: There are an estimated 3 million shipwrecks on the ocean floor — an underwater museum of human ambition and tragedy. From ancient Greek vessels to the Titanic, they preserve history in cold, dark water.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the Uluburun shipwreck (3,300 years old) and the Titanic wreck, then explain why deep-sea shipwrecks are so well preserved.

name: Marine Snow
teaser: A constant rain of organic debris falling from surface waters to the deep: dead plankton, fecal pellets, and mucus. Marine snow is the deep ocean's only food supply — and it sustains life thousands of meters down.

exploreAction.targetName: How the deep ocean gets its food
exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the biological pump and marine snow, then explain why deep-sea life depends entirely on what happens at the surface.

name: Cephalopod Intelligence
teaser: Octopuses solve puzzles, use tools, and escape from jars. Cuttlefish change color in milliseconds. Cephalopods are the ocean's most intelligent invertebrates — with three hearts and blue blood.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about octopus problem-solving (jar opening, maze navigation, coconut shell tool use), then explain why cephalopod intelligence evolved separately from vertebrate intelligence.

name: Nudibranchs
teaser: Sea slugs that steal: nudibranchs eat cnidarians and repurpose their stinging cells for their own defense. They're also some of the most photogenic creatures in the ocean — living jewels of the reef.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about kleptocnidae (stolen stinging cells), then find three visually stunning nudibranch species.

name: Sea Turtles
teaser: Navigation masters: sea turtles cross entire oceans to nest on the same beach where they were born. They've existed for 110 million years — surviving the asteroid that killed the dinosaurs.

exploreAction.targetName: How sea turtles navigate across oceans
exploreAction.instruction: Learn about magnetic navigation and natal homing, then find one threat to sea turtles and one conservation success.

name: How Little We've Explored
teaser: We've mapped the surface of Mars in more detail than the ocean floor. Only 20% of the seabed has been surveyed at high resolution. The deep ocean remains Earth's last true frontier.

exploreAction.instruction: Compare the percentage of ocean floor mapped vs. the surface of Mars and Moon, then explain why ocean exploration lags behind space exploration.

name: The Challenger Expedition
teaser: The first global oceanographic expedition (1872–1876): HMS Challenger traveled 130,000 km, discovered 4,700 new species, and measured the deepest ocean trenches. Modern ocean science began here.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the Challenger's instruments and discoveries, then explain why it's considered the birth of oceanography.

name: DSV Alvin
teaser: The submersible that discovered hydrothermal vents in 1977: Alvin has dove over 5,000 times, exploring the deep ocean from the Titanic wreck to mid-ocean ridges. It changed our understanding of life.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about Alvin's discovery of hydrothermal vent ecosystems, then find one other deep-sea discovery made with Alvin.

name: Sonar and Seafloor Mapping
teaser: Sound waves reveal the hidden landscape: multibeam sonar maps the ocean floor in detail, revealing mountains, trenches, and ridges we never knew existed. The ocean floor is more rugged than the land.

exploreAction.targetName: How we map the ocean floor
exploreAction.instruction: Learn about multibeam sonar and the Seabed 2030 project, then explain why mapping the ocean floor matters for climate science and navigation.
